1.pericope_label: Sheba’s revolt, and the ten concubines shut up for life

schools.summary: Henry makes the timing the lesson, the revolt following immediately on the crushing of Absalom, so that the end of one trouble proves the beginning of another and a reconciliation newly made needed handling tenderly, a broken bone once set requiring time to knit. He traces the occasion to the quarrel over who had most interest in bringing the king home, Israel pleading their numbers and Judah their kinship, and holds that David’s leaning to his own tribe is what drove Israel off; from which he draws that partiality is as impolitic in a prince as in a parent, that the hatred of inferiors may be feared whose love is despised, that the beginning of strife is as the letting forth of water, and that the perverting of words is the subverting of peace, since Judah said only that the king was near of kin and Israel heard that they had no part in him. He notes that Sheba was a Benjamite who dwelt in Mount Ephraim, and that he and Shimei were both of Saul’s tribe and both kept the old grudge of that house. On the concubines he gives three obligations together — duty, since they were now unclean to David; prudence, that the thing might not be so much as named; and justice, to punish them for an easy submission to Absalom’s lust while they despaired of the king’s return.

Gill glosses the man of Belial as a lawless and yokeless man who had cast off the yoke of the law, and holds that though with respect to second causes he may be said to have been there by chance, it was so ordered by providence for the further fulfilment of the threatening that the sword should not depart from David’s house. He has those who met the king on the road simply depart from him, and locates the palace in that part of the city called the fort of Zion.

Ellicott notes that the English follows the ancient versions in treating Bichri as a proper name whereas most recent commentators take it as a patronymic, the Bichrite, of the family of Becher the second son of Benjamin, which would put Sheba in Saul’s clan by descent; he places him at Gilgal with the representatives of the ten tribes, taking advantage of the dispute to renew Absalom’s rebellion, and hears in the cry to the tents the signal Jeroboam would afterwards use. He states the reversal of the tribes’ positions sharply: Judah, among whom the rebellion had originated and who had been tardy in returning to their allegiance, were now fierce in loyalty, while Israel, who had only joined an organised revolt and had afterwards been first to propose the king’s return, had become alienated. On the concubines he makes their state the necessary result under polygamy of what had happened, and allows the phrase to mean widowhood of life as the English has it or, with the Chaldee, widowhood of the living. Keil and Delitzsch guard the geography, holding that Judah’s cleaving to the king from Jordan does not prove the revolt broke out at the river before David reached Gilgal, since the phrase is explained by Judah having already fetched him across; and they read the shutting up as protective, that he brought the women into a place of safety and took care of them without going in to them again.

Clarke infers Sheba’s connection with Saul’s family from his being a Benjamite and confesses that nothing further is known of him, and renders the rebel cry as a repudiation of all obligation to the house of David. On the concubines he is alone in exculpating them: they were not in the transgression, so the king could not punish them, could not divorce them, could no more be familiar with them since they had been defiled, and could not safely marry them elsewhere, so he shut them up and fed them and made them quite comfortable. Wesley agrees that the man’s presence was casual in itself though ordered by God’s providence, reads the cry as a resolve to go home, consider, and meet to choose a new king, and hears contempt in the naming of David as the son of Jesse, as one no longer to be owned for king but reckoned a private person.

we have no part in David

4.pericope_label: Amasa commissioned and delayed; Abishai sent after Sheba

schools.summary: Henry sees both faces of the commission: the revolt let David keep his promise sooner than he could have wished, and promoting the man who had been the rebels’ own general was a real proof of the clemency of his government, but Joab’s envy and emulation made the keeping of it turn out ill for them both. He accounts for the delay by the backwardness of the men of Judah, who were forward enough to attend the king’s triumphs and backward to fight his battles, since most men love a loyalty, like a religion, that is cheap and easy; and he observes that had they pursued Sheba at once they might have crushed the thing in the egg. On the passing over of Joab he is the most pointed of the witnesses: David resolved to mortify and degrade him, not so much, he suspects, for the blood of Abner, which Joab shed basely, as for the blood of Absalom, which he shed justly and honourably — and he borrows bishop Hall on how slippery the stations of earthly honour are and how happy those in favour with him in whom there is no shadow of change.

Gill marks the commission as the public declaration of the generalship David had promised, and has Amasa go to gather the men out of their tribes to Jerusalem. He supposes David would have nothing to say to Joab, being displeased with him for slaying Absalom and having removed him from his posts, and so addressed the next officer — recording that Josephus has the king speak to Joab after all, contrary to the express words of the text. He notes that Joab, though out of the generalship, might still command a regiment.

Keil and Delitzsch call this first step toward fulfilling the promise a very imprudent act, like the promise itself, since Joab had commanded the army for years and was grievously offended, and since a well-tried general had incomparably more distinction in Judah than a man who had taken part in Absalom’s rebellion and even led its army. They suppose Amasa overstayed his time because the men of Judah distrusted him and were slow to answer, and they come down firmly on the disputed clause of David’s order: the figure is the apple of the eye, used elsewhere for a man’s most precious possession, so the sense is that Sheba will tear out our eye, that is, do us serious injury, and the gentler rendering that he will withdraw from our sight cannot be grammatically sustained — an explanation they credit to Böttcher. Ellicott judges the commission of very doubtful expediency at such a crisis, and is alone in reasoning from a geographical detail to the cause of the delay: since Amasa is met on his return at Gibeon he must have gone clear out of Judah into Benjamin and consumed the time by exceeding his instructions, which raises great doubt of his fitness for the place promised him — and he notes that Joab will presently insinuate the man was not really loyal. On the clause he reports that the English follows the Latin while the original is difficult and doubtful, others rendering that Sheba will pluck out our eye and the Greek that he will overshadow it, meaning either cause anxiety or hide where he cannot be found. He adds that Joab’s own corps would readily follow his brother, and that the mighty men appear to have been a particular body of heroes drawn chiefly from the companions of David’s outlaw years.

Clarke has David invest Amasa with the command and send him to collect the men of Judah and return within three days, and accounts for the delay by the muster proving harder than was at first supposed, which led David, fearing the rebellion would get head, to send Abishai — accompanied, as it appears, by Joab, who treacherously murdered Amasa when they met at Gibeon. Wesley offers a choice of two reasons for the delay, that the people were worn out by the late war and unwilling to begin another, or that the soldiers had more affection for Joab than for their new general; and he reads the choice of Abishai as a forward-looking caution, lest Joab should by this means recover his place, leaving Amasa discontented and David’s fidelity to his promise in question. He observes that Joab went along with the remainder of his army as a volunteer, watching an opportunity to do what he designed.

8.pericope_label: Joab murders Amasa at the great stone in Gibeon

schools.summary: Henry has the killing contrived down to the fittings: the coat girded close so as not to hang in the way, the belt over it so the sword lay ready to hand, and the weapon set in a sheath too large for it, so that a shake would spill it out as though by accident. He then anatomises the murder under six heads — that it was done subtly and by contrivance rather than on a sudden provocation; treacherously, under the pretence of a kinsman’s greeting, calling him brother and asking after his health while the drawn sword was in the other hand; impudently, at the head of the troops and in their sight, by a man too hardened in blood to blush or tremble; at a single blow, with so steady a hand that he needed not strike twice; in contempt of the commission David had given, so that the king was struck at through Amasa’s side; and unseasonably, when they were marching against a common enemy and needed to be unanimous, so that Joab could contentedly sacrifice the interest of king and kingdom to his personal revenge. He observes that Joab had done just so to Abner and gone unpunished, which encouraged him to do it again, and that covering blood with a cloth cannot stop its cry in God’s ear for vengeance.

Gill reports that the great stone was some five miles from Jerusalem on Josephus’s reckoning, that the place was appointed for the rendezvous, and that Amasa came there with the forces he had assembled and took the command of them. He has Joab speak in a friendly manner, with all the air of pleasantry and good humour; explains that Amasa took no heed of the sword because he had seen it drop and supposed Joab was returning it to the sheath, and so was not on his guard; and judges from the wallowing in the highway that the wound, though mortal, did not kill at once. He has the man posted by the body on Joab’s orders, to satisfy the people as they came up and keep the pursuit moving.

Ellicott reconstructs the trick soberly: a dagger was stuck in the girdle bound over the military coat, so arranged that it should fall as Joab advanced, and he picked it up naturally in his left hand while the right went out in greeting, so that his movements gave rise to no suspicion. He glosses the wound as in the abdomen, and remarks that Joab comes forward here as commander of the pursuit without previous mention, having either marched out with Abishai or joined him on the road, and that he assumed his old place after the killing with his brother’s connivance; his real motive, as with Abner, was personal jealousy and ambition. He reads the battle cry left with the body as a suggestion that Amasa had rightly been put to death for his doubtful loyalty, and supposes the people who stood still were the very levies Amasa had been raising, paralysed at the sight of the leader the king had just promoted wallowing in his blood. Keil and Delitzsch describe the mechanism without imputing the design, construing the clause to mean that the sheath came out of the sword-belt in which it was fastened and the sword fell to the ground, and noting that the verse consists only of circumstantial clauses; they too remark on the oddity of Joab’s appearing among the force, and as its commander, without explanation.

Clarke alone preserves a rival account of the sword, that some of the versions and able critics take the words to mean Joab stumbled, the weapon falling as he tripped, and that he took it up left-handed as a man with no bad intention would, before seizing Amasa’s beard with the right and ripping up his bowels with the left; he notes that the garment was not a military one and that the short sword was so loose in its sheath as to be easily drawn, and remarks that in the East it is the beard, not the man, which is kissed. He holds that the word rendered the fifth rib means any part of the abdominal region, the Greek giving the groin and the Targum the thigh, and adds from his own experience that a man may live some hours after his bowels have been shed out. He renders the proclamation as a plain statement that there is now no other commander, and that Joab is steadily attached to David, so let the loyal follow him. Wesley takes the fall of the sword to have been contrived, so that at the least motion of Joab’s body it should drop and he might take it up without raising suspicion; he explains why nobody avenged Amasa, partly because few of his men had yet come up and partly because Joab’s authority with the soldiers, especially David’s guards, was very great and they had no kindness for a man who had been general of the rebel army and whom they might think unfit for so great a trust; and he ends where Henry does, that covering blood with a cloth cannot stop its cry to God for vengeance.

14.pericope_label: Sheba besieged in Abel, and a wise woman calls from the wall

schools.summary: Henry has Sheba ramble over all the tribes and find them less willing on second thoughts than they had been in a sudden provocation, so that he gathered only a few like himself — one bad man, as Henry puts it, will find or make more — and took shelter in a strong city of the north in the lot of Naphtali, his adherents being mostly men of Beeroth in Benjamin. He holds that the place was justly attacked which dared to harbour a traitor, and turns it on the heart that indulges rebellious lusts which will not have Christ reign over them. On the woman he is the fullest of the witnesses: not one of the men of Abel, none of its elders or magistrates, offered to treat with Joab even at the last extremity, whether from stupidity, or awe of Sheba, or despair of terms, or want of sense to manage a treaty, and this one woman’s wisdom saved the city — from which he argues that souls know no difference of sexes, that though the man be the head it does not follow that he has the monopoly of the brains, that many a masculine heart and more than masculine has been found in a female breast, and that the treasure of wisdom is no less valuable for being lodged in the weaker vessel. He supposes it was the first time Joab had ever treated with a woman in martial affairs.

Gill takes the going through all the tribes of Sheba, canvassing for a party or else fleeing from place to place, and reports the minority reading against himself: Josephus understands it of Joab pursuing him, and the Syriac and Arabic versions and R. Isaiah read it so too, though he judges the first sense more generally received. He has Joab and Abishai pursue him to the city and besiege him there, compares the woman with the woman of Tekoah, reports the supposition of some that she was the city’s governess, and has her cry with a loud voice from the wall to Joab’s men who were battering it beneath her.

Ellicott identifies Abel with a village still standing north-west of Lake Huleh whose byname celebrates the excellence of its wheat, notes that the preposition in the English name should be dropped, that the place is named with Ijon and Dan elsewhere, and that it is called Abel of waters in Chronicles to distinguish it from other places of the same name, lying at the extreme north of the land. Of Sheba’s followers he says they were apparently a family or clan in the north otherwise entirely unknown, that the Greek and Latin here seem to follow a different text, and that the conjecture making the word a form of the term for fortresses must be rejected since no such form is known. He explains the trench as the space between the city wall and the lower outer wall, so that planting the mounds for the battering engines there was already an important advantage. Keil and Delitzsch describe the rampart piled up until it rose by the town-moat with its low wall, while all the people with Joab battered to throw the wall down; they find in the woman’s opening proverb the evidence that Abel had formerly been celebrated for the wisdom of its inhabitants, and explain the plural predicate of her self-description on the ground that she spoke in the city’s name as well as in its favour, the figure of a mother standing for the capital.

Clarke places Beth-maachah in the northern part of the land on the confines of Syria and probably in Naphtali, and is alone in supposing Abel the capital of the district Luke calls Abilene. On the siege works he denies that the word rendered bank means a bank at all, taking it most probably for a battering engine or a tower overlooking the walls, from which archers and slingers could annoy the inhabitants while others sapped below, and arguing that a mere bank could not be described as standing in the trench. Of the woman he says in one line that she was probably governess. Wesley explains the longer name as distinguishing this Abel from others and marking it as the one on the northern border toward that part of Syria called Maachah, makes the Berites men of Beeroth of Benjamin who adhered to Sheba as of the same tribe and perhaps the same city, and keeps the bank as a platform from which to batter the wall or shoot at its defenders, standing in or near the trench so that the city was in great danger. On the woman he follows Henry closely, that none of the men of Abel offered to treat and one wise woman saved the city, since souls know no difference of sex and many a manly heart is lodged in a female breast.

18.pericope_label: The woman’s plea, Joab’s terms, and Sheba’s head over the wall

schools.summary: Henry takes the proverb in the sense of the margin, that the besiegers ought to have demanded the traitor before storming the place, so that she tacitly upbraids Joab for not offering peace; and he sets out her whole argument in four points — that the city was long so famed for prudent men that it was the common referee of the country, that its people were peaceable and faithful and had taken no part in sedition, that it was a mother in Israel and part of the inheritance of the Lord whose destruction would weaken the nation God had chosen, and that the law of war required peace to be offered first. He observes that Joab, though he had lately destroyed Amasa in a private quarrel, would by no means bear the imputation of delighting in bloodshed when acting as a general, and draws the practical moral from the double misunderstanding, that the city held out believing he aimed at its ruin while he attacked believing the citizens were Sheba’s confederates, so that a great deal of mischief would be prevented if contending parties would understand one another. On the terms he turns the single condition into a figure of God’s dealing with a besieged soul: sin is the traitor, the beloved lust is the rebel, and there is no peace on any other terms. He notes that Joab knew the traitor’s face and looked no further, wishing none of the adherents to suffer, and went back with the trophies rather of peace than of victory.

Gill treats the saying as a proverbial expression among the ancient sages, and reads her self-description as spoken for a city made up of men peaceable among themselves and faithful to their king, never concerned in any insurrection, not even the late one under Absalom. He has Joab repeat his disclaimer to show how detestable the suggestion was to him, and has the woman go down from the wall into the city, convene the principal inhabitants, and so represent the matter that they unanimously agreed to her motion.

Ellicott judges the simplest explanation of the proverb the true one, that Abel had become proverbial for its wisdom, but preserves an ancient Jewish interpretation taken into the Targum which turns the words into a reproach, asking whether Joab has done what the law requires and asked the city for peace at the first. He explains the range of hills from which Sheba came as so named because much of it lay in Ephraim though it extended south into Benjamin, and quotes the judgment that Joab’s character comes out strongly in the transaction — politic, decided, bold and unscrupulous, but never needlessly cruel or impulsive or even revengeful, so that no life is safe which stands in his way, while from policy he never sacrifices the most insignificant life without a purpose. Keil and Delitzsch say the woman’s words made an impression on Joab and that he felt the truthfulness of her reproaches, render his disclaimer as an oath formula, note that the hill country named extended into Benjamin, and have her come to the citizens with the very counsel she had given Joab and which he had accepted, whereupon they cut off Sheba’s head and threw it out, and Joab blew the trumpet for a retreat and returned to the king.

Clarke is the most sceptical about the proverb: its origin is unknown, much must be supplied to bring it to speak sense, and though Abel was probably famed for the wisdom of its inhabitants, so that parties in dispute appealed to their judgment as final by consent, he goes no further than that — adding that the woman intimates Joab should have proceeded in that way before storming the city and destroying peaceable inhabitants. He thinks she speaks in the city’s name throughout, so that a mother in Israel means a chief city of a district rather than anything about the speaker, and infers from the promise she makes that she had great sway in the counsels of the city; he observes that beheading was then the punishment of a state rebel, as it still is. Wesley expands the proverb into the practice of neighbours agreeing to stand by the arbitration of the men of Abel, explains that great cities are called mothers as the dependent towns are called daughters, and presses the case that the woman held office, since though the work was commonly men’s, women were sometimes employed in government, as Deborah judged Israel. He supposes the hill country named was rather a place within Benjamin, so called either from the Ephraimite border or from some notable action of the Ephraimites there.

23.pericope_label: David’s ministers of state after the risings were quelled

schools.summary: Henry gives the state of David’s court after his restoration: Joab kept the command, being too great to be displaced, and Benaiah as before was captain of the guards. He picks out the one office erected since the earlier list, that of treasurer or officer over the tribute, and remarks that it was not till toward the latter end of his time that David began to raise taxes, and that the man who held it held it long and that it cost him his life at last. He closes on the plain application, that it is well when able men are appointed to discharge public duties, and that all should seek to perform those duties as faithful servants to the Son of David.

Gill is uncertain whether Joab was ever actually displaced, offering both accounts — that David thought to do it and was not able, because of Joab’s power and influence with the people, or that he had done it, as some things in the chapter seem to show, and judged it most advisable to replace a man whom Amasa’s death and the quelling of the rebellion had made more haughty and more popular still. He explains the occasion of the list, that mention of Joab as established over the whole army drew in an account of the rest, the more so as this was a sort of beginning of the reign anew after the risings; makes the tribute cover both the revenue from David’s own people and the tribute of the conquered nations, with the Targum understanding the officer to be over those who collected and brought it; and on the last name canvasses three identifications — the Ithrite, the son of Ikkesh of Tekoah as the Targum has it, or his own preference, a descendant of Jair of Gilead who was perhaps a friend to David there — reporting also the etymology that derives the name from a root meaning to enlighten.

Keil and Delitzsch give the source-critical account: the second section of David’s history closes with a list of leading ministers as the first did, and the author evidently found both lists in his sources and included them because they belonged to different periods and supplemented one another, as the difference in some of the names shows; this list belongs to a later period, and adds to the earlier one an officer over the tribute and a confidential counsellor in the place of the sons of David named before. Ellicott notes that nearly all the officers here are the same as in the earlier roll, and that the scribe appears under a different name there. On the tribute he dissents from the others: the word should rather be rendered the levy, the forced labour afterwards so largely employed by Solomon, and he finds it remarkable that neither the earlier list nor its parallel in Chronicles shows any trace of the post, which was a feature of oriental despotism introduced only toward the close of David’s reign and carried much further under his son; he adds that men of nearly the same name held the office under Solomon and at the beginning of the next reign, perhaps all one person or at least of one family. Of the last officer he says he is named in no other list, that an Ira the Ithrite stands among the thirty and seven but there is no ground for identifying the two, and that the post had earlier been held by David’s own sons, so that the murder of the eldest, Absalom’s rebellion and death, and other disorders in that household had apparently led to a change.

Clarke states the position without softening it: Joab had murdered Amasa and seized the supreme command, and such was his power and the service he had rendered in quelling the rebellion that David was obliged to continue him and dared not call him to account for his murders without endangering the state by a civil war. He makes Benaiah’s charge the archers and slingers, the officer over the tribute the chief receiver of taxes or chancellor of the exchequer, and the recorder the registrar of public events. On the last title he notes that the Hebrew is literally a priest to David, which the Latin, Greek, Syriac and Arabic all follow, while the Chaldee makes him a prince or chief, and guesses a sort of domestic chaplain, comparing the seers whom the kings of Judah kept. Wesley accounts for Joab’s retention by the good success of this expedition and the former, which had so fixed his interest in the army and among David’s fastest friends that the king could not without danger displace him.
